---
title: "How a Lesson Works"
subtitle: "What each piece is for, and what you do before, during, and after class"
---

## Who Each Piece Is For

| Piece | Who uses it | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Lesson plan** | You, the teacher | Before class to prepare; during class as your script |
| **Slides** | The whole class, projected | During class |
| **`.py` files and notebooks** | Students, on their own computers | During class, and for practice |
| **Practice** | Students | After each lesson (homework or the next class's start) |
| **Assignment** | Students | Near the end of each module |
| **Answer keys and marking notes** | You only | Not on this site; in the `answer-keys` folder of the course's GitHub repository |

The lesson plans look interactive because they contain the same step-through boxes and runnable code that appear on the slides. That lets you try every activity yourself before class. **The lesson plan is for you, not for students.** Students work from the slides, the code files, and the practice pages.

## The Cycle

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart TD
  A["Before class:<br/>read the plan, run the examples"] --> B["In class:<br/>slides; read, predict, run"]
  B --> C["After class:<br/>practice; read exit tickets"]
  C --> D["Next class:<br/>review from the exit tickets"]
  D --> B
  C -. "end of module" .-> E["Assignment and test"]
```

### Before class

1. Read the lesson plan, starting with **At a Glance**. Note the **teacher prompts**: what to say aloud the first time students meet a tool or idea.
2. Run every example on **your** computer and note what it reports. Answers depend on the computer.
3. Check that students can open the slides and run Python (see [Before You Begin](before-you-begin.qmd)).

### In class (75 minutes)

Use two screens: the **slides on the projector** and the **lesson plan on your own laptop**. Press **S** in the slides to open speaker view, which shows the teacher prompts on your screen only. Each slide deck has a link back to its lesson plan at the bottom.

Follow the lesson plan's timings. Every lesson follows the same rhythm:

| Stage | What happens | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Review or warm-up | Short retrieval or guessing questions | Slides |
| Teach | You read a worked example aloud and trace it | Slides, your computer |
| Predict, then run | Students write a prediction, then step through the code | Slides; students' computers |
| Investigate | Trace tables and line-by-line questions | Slides; students copy tables into their tracing notebooks |
| Modify | Students change working code | Students' computers |
| Make | Students write a little code of their own | Students' computers |
| Check | Exit ticket: one short reading question | Slides, paper |

### After class

- Students complete that lesson's **practice** (linked from the last slide and from each module page). Practice also starts with reading: predict, then run.
- Read the exit tickets. Use what they show to choose the next class's review questions.

### What to give students

The whole site is public, so students *can* open the lesson plans. They don't reveal quiz answers, but they do show what's coming next. In your learning management system, share the **slides** and **practice** links (and the **assignment** at the end of the module), and keep the lesson plans for yourself.

The step-through boxes are cramped on a phone. In class, students should use a computer.

### Where students write answers

- **Tracing notebook:** every student keeps a paper notebook for predictions, trace tables, and short answers, in class and on Practice pages. Tracing by hand is the point, and there's nothing to save or lose. (It's called a *tracing* notebook so it isn't confused with Jupyter notebooks.)
- **Anything handed in:** written answers go in comments in the `.py` file, at the top. Assignments come with a starter file that has a space for every answer.
- The prediction box in the step-through boxes isn't saved. It keeps the prediction next to the real output while students compare.

### Handing In Work {#handing-in-work}

**On day one,** students follow [Set Up Your Course Folder](course-folder.qmd): an `ics3u` folder in their home folder with a sub-folder for each module and lesson. Check it in Lesson 2; it saves a lot of "I can't find my file" later.

**What gets handed in, and in what format:**

| Work | Format | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lesson Make programs (optional) | `.py` file | Written answers in a comment at the top, output pasted at the bottom |
| Quick Builds | `.py` file | Small graded programs, two per module |
| Module assignments: the code | Starter `.py` file | Has a space for every short answer |
| Module assignments: longer written parts | Document (planned) | Test plans, structure charts, the Module 4 protection plan, write-ups |
| Module 7 project documents | Document (planned) | Specification, Gantt chart, test plan, status reports |
| Research report (Computer Science in the World) | Student's choice | Website, slides, or video |
| Practice pages | Not collected | Tracing notebook; spot-check as you circulate |

**Not everything is Python.** Code and short answers belong in the `.py` file, but longer writing and tables are easier in a document. Downloadable **Word** documents (which also open in Google Docs) and **fillable PDFs** are planned for these parts. Until they arrive, students can use a Word or Google Docs copy of the instructions.

**Jupyter notebooks** are fine where your class uses Colab or the Callysto Hub: students answer in text cells and hand in the `.ipynb` file. Remember that notebooks online report a different computer.

**Practical tips:**

- Pick one file-naming rule, such as `lastname_m01_report_card.py`, and use it all year. Your learning management system may rename files anyway; a clear name still helps when you download them all.
- Download a whole class's submissions into one folder and run each program. Most marking starts with "does it run?"
- From Module 6 on, students generate their own sample folder with their own seed, so each student's output is different.

### End of module

- Students complete the module **assignment**, which brings the module's ideas together in one program.
- A module test (not on this site) always includes a code-reading and tracing section.

## Formats

Practice and assignments live on this site because they're interactive: students predict, step through, and run code right on the page. Downloadable versions (Google Docs, Word, or PDF) may be added later for printing or for a learning management system.
